In the early phase of thinking about advanced technologies, nanotechnology was seen as one of the most powerful scientific
developments. It refers to the manipulation of matter at an extremely small scale, such as atoms and molecules. During the early 2000s,
some scientists and engineers proposed very ambitious ideas about what nanotechnology could achieve in the future. One of the most
famous contributors to this vision was K. Eric Drexler, who suggested that tiny machines, called nanobots, could one day build almost
anything by arranging atoms one by one.


These ideas created huge excitement because they seemed to offer solutions to many human problems. Nanobots were imagined as
machines that could cure diseases, remove poverty, and even extend human life significantly. Some extreme versions of this vision also
suggested that humans could transfer their minds into machines and achieve a form of digital immortality. Along with this optimism, there
were also serious fears. One major concern was the idea of "grey goo," a scenario in which self-replicating nanobots could multiply
uncontrollably and consume all matter on Earth.


However, as scientific understanding improved, these ideas came under strong criticism. Researchers pointed out that such visions were
not supported by real scientific evidence. At the molecular level, matter does not behave like mechanical systems such as gears or
machines. Instead, it is governed by complex chemical interactions and random motion, which makes precise control at that level
extremely difficult.


In reality, nanotechnology has developed in a much more limited and practical direction. Instead of building tiny robots, scientists have
focused on using chemistry and materials science to create useful applications. These include developments in medicine, electronics, and
imaging technologies. While these advancements are important, they are far less dramatic than the original futuristic predictions.


Many technological visions are shaped more by imagination than by actual scientific possibility. These ideas often promise perfect futures
without suffering, death, or limitations, which makes them attractive but unrealistic. Such exaggerated predictions can sometimes distract
attention from real scientific progress that solves practical problems.


Today, similar patterns can be seen in discussions about other emerging technologies as well. Bold claims and fears often develop faster
than actual scientific progress. Therefore, it becomes important to carefully evaluate such ideas and separate realistic science from
speculative imagination.


(360 words, by No suffering, no death, no limits: the nanobots pipe dream)

Niccolao Manucci was a Venetian traveller who came to India in the 17th century and spent most of his life there. He is known for writing
one of the earliest European accounts of the Mughal Empire called Storia do Mogor. His work is considered valuable because it provides
detailed descriptions of Mughal rulers, court life, and everyday customs in India during that period. Manucci travelled across many regions
of India, worked under different rulers, and also served in roles such as soldier, physician, and interpreter.


Manucci's travel account is important for historians because it gives first-hand observations of political events and social life in Mughal
India. He wrote about major figures like Aurangzeb, Shah Jahan, and Dara Shikoh. However, his writings are not always fully reliable.
Scholars have pointed out that his memoir contains both factual information and exaggerated or inaccurate details. This makes it
necessary for historians to carefully verify his claims using other sources.


Despite these limitations, Manucci's work remains significant because very few Europeans lived in India for such a long period during that
time. He observed not only royal courts but also local customs, traditions, and everyday life of people. His writings include descriptions of
food habits, social practices, and cultural differences between Europeans and Indians. These details help modern researchers understand
historical India beyond just political history.

[[PAGE 3]]
Manucci's life in India was full of movement and change. He worked with different rulers and communities, which allowed him to
experience diverse regions and cultures. Eventually, he settled in southern India, where he continued writing his memoirs. His travelogue
was later published in Europe and became an important historical source for studying the Mughal period.


Overall, Manucci's account is both valuable and complex. While it provides rare historical insight, it must be read critically due to its mix of
accurate observation and personal interpretation.

There was no hope for him this time: it was the third stroke. Night after night I had passed the house (it was vacation time) and studied the
lighted square of window: and night after night I had found it lighted in the same way, faintly and evenly. If he was dead, I thought, I would
see the reflection of candles on the darkened blind for I knew that two candles must be set at the head of a corpse. He had often said to
me: "I am not long for this world," and I had thought his words idle. Now I knew they were true. Every night as I gazed up at the window I
said softly to myself the word paralysis. It had always sounded strangely in my ears, like the word gnomon in the Euclid and the word
simony in the Catechism. But now it sounded to me like the name of some maleficent and sinful being. It filled me with fear, and yet I
longed to be nearer to it and to look upon its deadly work.


Old Cotter was sitting at the fire, smoking, when I came downstairs to supper. While my aunt was ladling out my stirabout he said, as if
returning to some former remark of his:


"No, I wouldn't say he was exactly ... but there was something queer ... there was something uncanny about him. I'll tell you my opinion...."


He began to puff at his pipe, no doubt arranging his opinion in his mind. Tiresome old fool! When we knew him first he used to be rather

[[PAGE 5]]
interesting, talking of faints and worms; but I soon grew tired of him and his endless stories about the distillery.


"I have my own theory about it," he said. "I think it was one of those ... peculiar cases.... But it's hard to say...."


He began to puff again at his pipe without giving us his theory. My uncle saw me staring and said to me:


"Well, so your old friend is gone, you'll be sorry to hear."


"Who?" said I.


"Father Flynn."

Looking back, we will remember 2025 as the year of the great capitulation. It was the year liberal democracy lost its nerve, as law firms,
universities, media organizations, corporations and countries appeased an increasingly illiberal United States in an unseemly and
miscalculated scramble to get the best possible deals for themselves.

bargaining chips you have, including retaliating when you are attacked.

already underway. It began in countries like my own and Australia, where what had seemed like likely election victories for the populist
right were stymied by a surge of patriotic resistance. A few months later, Norway and the Netherlands followed suit.

An elated NASA on April 10, 2026 was celebrating its successful voyage around the Moon, after four astronauts safely returned to Earth
having completed the first lunar flyby in more than 50 years. The NASA spacecraft carrying four astronauts - three Americans and one
Canadian - splashed down without a hitch off the California coast, capping the US space agency's crewed test mission that returned with
spectacular images of the Moon. From liftoff to splashdown, the trip clocked in at nine days, one hour, 31 minutes and 35 seconds -
though NASA rounds up and calls it a 10-day mission. It began with a dramatic launch from Florida on April 1, and was studded with firsts,
records and extraordinary moments. The four astronauts become the humans to travel furthest away from the Earth, at 252,756 miles
(406,771 kilometers). While hurtling through deep space and zipping around the Moon they took thousands of photographs, amassing a
stunning portfolio of images that captivated people on Earth. They also witnessed a solar eclipse along with extraordinary meteorite
strikes on the lunar surface. Several achievements added to the voyage's historic nature: Mr. Glover was the first person of color to fly
around the Moon, Ms. Koch was the first woman, and Canadian Hansen the first non-American.


NASA is hoping it can put boots on the lunar surface as soon as 2028 -- the final full year of Trump's second White House term. Experts,
however, have voiced skepticism that the lunar landers being developed by SpaceX and Blue Origin, companies owned by billionaires Elon
Musk and Jeff Bezos respectively, will be ready in time. China, meanwhile, is forging ahead with its own effort targeting 2030 to put
astronauts on the Moon. In the meantime, NASA is hoping to capitalize on the Artemis II mission's success to drum up excitement about
space exploration. Clayton Swope, a space policy expert at of the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told AFP that the mission
stands as "proof that when America keeps its eye on the prize, it can still do very great things."

The Census 2027, world's largest census exercise has begun. The Government of India has commenced Phase I of Census 2027 -
Houselisting and Housing Census (HLO) from today, marking the beginning of the country's largest administrative and statistical exercise.
This is India's first ever digital data capture and Self-Enumeration. The national enumeration exercise was initiated with the enumeration of
the President of India, Smt Droupadi Murmu, through the option of Self-Enumeration, upholding the proud tradition of commencing the
national count with the First Citizen of India. The Vice-President, Shri C.P. Radhakrishnan filled out the self-enumeration form online for
Census 2027, at Uprashtrapati Bhavan. The Prime Minister, Shri Narendra Modi completed his self-enumeration. Prime Minister appealed
to the people of India to self-enumerate their household details themselves and participate in the Census process.


In the first phase of rollout, Self-Enumeration process has commenced in eight States and Union Territories including Andaman and
Nicobar Islands, Goa, Karnataka, Lakshadweep, Mizoram, Odisha, Sikkim, New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC) area and Delhi
Cantonment Board of the National Capital from 1st April 2026. About 55,000 households from these States/UTs availed Self-Enumeration
facility on the very first day.The Houselisting and Housing Census in these States/UTs will begin from April 16, 2026 and will continue till
May 15, 2026. The Self-Enumeration exercise is a secure, web-based facility available in 16 regional languages. For the first time,
respondents can fill in their details online at their convenience before the enumerator's visit. Enumerators will carry out door-to-door visits
in all allocated houselisitng blocks as in previous Censuses, while Self-Enumeration serves as an additional facility. To participate in Self-
Enumeration, respondents can log in to the portal se.census.gov.in using their mobile number and basic credentials. Upon successful
submission, a unique Self-Enumeration ID (SE ID) is generated, which will be shared with the enumerator during the subsequent field visit

[[PAGE 11]]
for confirmation. During the Houselisting and Housing Census phase, comprehensive information on the condition of housing, household
amenities and assets possessed will be collected. A total of 33 questions for Phase I have been notified in January 2026 to capture these
critical indicators, which serve as the foundation for evidence-based planning, policy formulation, and targeted welfare interventions.

The emergence of generative AI has posed significant doctrinal and ethical challenges to copyright law, particularly in jurisdictions
governed by statutes such as the Copyright Act, 1957. Copyright protects "original works of authorship," requiring a minimal degree of
creativity and, traditionally, human authorship. However, AI systems are trained on massive datasets, often scraped from the internet,
which may include copyrighted works used without express authorization.


A central legal issue is whether such use constitutes infringement or falls within exceptions like "fair dealing" under Section 52 of the Act.
Courts have historically interpreted fair dealing narrowly, focusing on purpose, character, and market impact. While AI developers argue
that training is "transformative," critics assert that large-scale, non-consensual ingestion of copyrighted material may substitute the
original market or unjustly exploit creators' economic rights. Authorship presents another doctrinal challenge. Copyright law presumes a
human author; hence, fully autonomous AI-generated works may fail to qualify for protection. However, where a human exercises creative
control through detailed prompts, selection, arrangement, or substantial editing, the output may satisfy the originality threshold. Ethically,
concerns arise regarding transparency, attribution, and bias. The opaque nature of AI training complicates identifying whose works were
used and whether consent or compensation was provided. Scholars argue for a regulatory framework that ensures accountability while
fostering innovation. Thus, the evolving legal landscape must reconcile statutory principles with technological realities, balancing the
protection of creators with the advancement of AI.

Passage – 2


Section 26 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872 renders void every agreement in restraint of the marriage of any person, other than a minor.
The provision is founded on public policy that treats the freedom to marry as an essential personal liberty. Courts have consistently

[[PAGE 16]]
interpreted this rule strictly: both absolute and partial restraints-whether based on time, person, class, or circumstance-are void if they
substantially interfere with the choice to marry.


However, the application of this principle often turns on whether a condition constitutes a real restraint or merely an incidental or
regulatory provision. Courts have, in certain cases, upheld conditions that affect property or conduct, provided they do not operate as a
direct prohibition or deterrent against marriage. The distinction is subtle: a condition that merely postpones enjoyment of a benefit without
penalizing marriage may be treated differently from one that withdraws or forfeits a benefit upon marriage.


Further complexity arises in the context of minors. Section 26 expressly excludes minors, not to validate restraints on their marriage, but
because minors lack contractual capacity. Issues concerning child marriage are governed instead by the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act,
2006, under which a child marriage is generally voidable at the option of the minor, except in specified aggravated circumstances where it
is void ab initio. Thus, while contract law does not directly invalidate restraints concerning minors, it does not endorse them either.


The interplay of these principles requires careful evaluation of the substance, effect, and surrounding context of each condition. The law
does not merely look at the form of the agreement but examines whether the condition, in practical terms, discourages or restricts
marriage.

The modern law of the sea is primarily governed by the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which establishes a
comprehensive framework regulating maritime zones, state rights, and navigation freedoms. Coastal states exercise varying degrees of
control over different maritime zones measured from their baseline, typically the low-water line along the coast.


Within territorial waters, extending up to 12 nautical miles, the coastal state enjoys full sovereignty, subject only to the right of "innocent
passage" granted to foreign vessels. Passage is considered innocent so long as it is not prejudicial to the peace, good order, or security of
the coastal state. Activities such as weapons exercises, spying, or fishing may render passage non-innocent. Beyond this lies the
contiguous zone, extending up to 24 nautical miles, where the coastal state may enforce laws relating to customs, taxation, immigration,
and sanitation.Further outward is the Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ), extending up to 200 nautical miles, where the coastal state has
sovereign rights for the purpose of exploring, exploiting, conserving, and managing natural resources. However, other states retain
freedoms of navigation and overflight in the EEZ. The high seas, lying beyond national jurisdiction, are governed by the principle of
freedom of the seas. No state may validly claim sovereignty over any part of the high seas, and all states enjoy freedoms including
navigation, fishing, and scientific research, subject to certain international obligations. Conflicts often arise when states attempt to extend
control beyond permissible limits or when the nature of an activity such as surveillance or resource extraction blurs the distinction
between lawful use and violation of coastal state rights. The resolution of such disputes depends on interpreting the balance between
sovereignty and shared global commons.

The guarantee of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution of India constitutes a foundational pillar of
constitutional democracy, enabling the circulation of ideas, dissent, and critique. However, this guarantee is carefully structured rather than
absolute. Under Article 19(2) of the Constitution of India, the State may impose reasonable restrictions on this freedom in the interests of
sovereignty and integrity of India, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of
court, defamation, and incitement to an offence.


Judicial interpretation has consistently emphasized that restrictions must satisfy a test of reasonableness and proportionality, requiring a
proximate nexus between the expression and the harm sought to be prevented. For instance, restrictions based on public order must
demonstrate a direct and imminent threat rather than speculative or remote consequences. Similarly, the ground of security of the State is
invoked only in cases involving serious threats such as rebellion or insurrection, and not mere criticism of government policies. The
limitation based on decency or morality, particularly in cases of obscenity, has evolved over time. Courts assess whether the expression,
taken as a whole, tends to deprave or corrupt, while also considering artistic, literary, or social value. The mere presence of explicit content
does not automatically justify restriction if the larger message is socially relevant.


The ground of defamation protects individual reputation against false and harmful statements, while contempt of court seeks to preserve
the authority and integrity of the judiciary by restricting publications that may scandalize or prejudice judicial proceedings. Further,
restrictions based on incitement to an offence require a close connection between the speech and the likelihood of unlawful action.

The first set of talks in Islamabad provided a sense of Iran's internal tensions. Iranian delegations dispatched for talks with America are
usually lean, disciplined and tightly briefed. The Islamabad one was anything but: it was composed of some 80 Iranians. They ranged from
a seasoned diplomat who helped fine-tune a nuclear deal with the Obama administration in 2015, to a firebrand who derides America as "a
vicious yellow dog" and sneers that any deal would be capitulation. Their arguments were so ferocious that Pakistani mediators are
reported to have spent as much time refereeing among the Iranians as engaging the Americans.


One cause of the tensions is the existence of a vacuum at the top. Seven weeks after an American-Israeli air strike killed Ali Khamenei, the
supreme leader for 37 years, his successors have failed to find a date for his funeral. His son and designated successor, Mojtaba
Khamenei, is thought to be either incapacitated or too weak to impose authority.


Since a ceasefire was declared on April 8th, the regime's wartime cohesion has begun to fray. Formally, authority rests with the Supreme
National Security Council. Mohammad-Bagher Ghalibaf, the speaker, has been designated as chief negotiator, with Mr Araghchi as his
lieutenant. But their readiness to negotiate has provoked a backlash, particularly from the IRGC, the 190,000-strong force that defends the
Islamic Republic.


Inside Iran, signs of swelling military assertiveness are plentiful. Pro-regime crowds have taken to denouncing Mr Araghchi and Mr
Ghalibaf by name. Military communiqués delivered by men in fatigues appear to have replaced clerical sermons. Some argue that the
cacophony is tactical-a way to extract concessions by projecting hardline opposition. Yet the war appears to be hardening a new faultline
between nationalists who are guided by realpolitik and state interest, and Islamists who are anchored in revolutionary ideology.


Material interests muddy matters further. Over the years a class of generals-turned-sanction-busters has emerged: its members are
thought to benefit handsomely from operations to circumvent American sanctions on the economy. With Khamenei senior gone,
previously sidelined figures have re-emerged. Each group has a different view on the most important sticking-points in the talks, including
the nuclear programme, control of Gulf waters and the role of Iran's regional proxies. Nationalists would trade proxy networks for
sanctions relief; Islamists see them as the spine of "resistance".


Even if Iran returns to talks, the deep divisions within the Iranian delegation mean both that it will be hard to reach a deal, and that any
agreement with America could quickly unravel.

The special session of Parliament to consider the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 - and also the Union Territories Laws
(Amendment) Bill, 2026, and the Delimitation Bill, 2026 - for readjustment of Lok Sabha and Legislative Assembly seats across the country
and implementation of reservation of seats for women ended in a spectacular way. The proposed delimitation was to reallocate the
number of Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly seats among States, and determine the territorial boundaries of each constituency,
based on data from the 2011 Census. The total number of Lok Sabha seats was proposed to be increased to 850. The special session was
convened at a time when electioneering for the ongoing Legislative Assembly elections is at its peak in West Bengal and Tamil Nadu.


Articles 82 and 170 (3) of the Constitution require a readjustment of the number of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats in each State and the
extent of every constituency, after each Census. The first delimitation exercise in independent India was carried out in 1950-51 by the
Election Commission of India. After the completion of the first general election, a fresh delimitation did take place based on the 1951
Census. Subsequently, readjustment of constituencies was carried out after the Census in 1961 and 1971. The delimitation based on the
1971 Census was completed in 1976.


The Forty-Second Amendment of the Constitution froze further delimitation until the Census of 2001. It was intended to ensure that States
successfully curbing population growth were not disadvantaged in terms of representation, while States with higher population growth did
not gain a corresponding increase in seats.


The temporary freeze on delimitation ended in 2001. However, the government decided to redraw the territories of constituencies to
ensure inter se parity in terms of population across them. The Constitutional provisions were amended to provide that territories of the

[[PAGE 27]]
constituencies would be readjusted on the basis of the 2001 Census figures without altering the number of seats.


The Statement of Objects and Reasons in the Bill for the Constitution (Eighty-fourth Amendment) Act, 2001 stated that the government
decided to extend the freeze on undertaking fresh delimitation up to the year 2026. As per the provisions of Articles 82 and 170(3), the
freeze on further delimitation is to be in place until the population figures of the first Census to be taken after 2026 are published.


The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the current Delimitation Bill, 2026 noted that population growth and migration "have resulted in
varying density of population in electoral constituencies"; the Bill sought to address this issue. However, the population figures of the 2011
Census were to be adopted.


There is nothing to suggest that migration has either stopped or slowed since 2011, or that population growth has stabilised uniformly
across all regions. It was quite likely that when constituencies are finally carved out, many of them would exhibit real-time disparities when
compared with the principles set out in the present Bill.

decided to extend the freeze on undertaking fresh delimitation up to the year 2026. As per the provisions of Articles 82 and 170(3), the
freeze on further delimitation is to be in place until the population figures of the first Census to be taken after 2026 are published.


The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the current Delimitation Bill, 2026 noted that population growth and migration "have resulted in
varying density of population in electoral constituencies"; the Bill sought to address this issue. However, the population figures of the 2011
Census were to be adopted.

across all regions. It was quite likely that when constituencies are finally carved out, many of them would exhibit real-time disparities when
compared with the principles set out in the present Bill.

three types of AI tools such as Generative AI (GenAI) for content and code creation, Predictive AI for demand forecasting and risk
assessment, and Process Automation AI (PA-AI) for repetitive back-office tasks.


Operations was the largest department, accounting for 5/12 of the total workforce, followed by Sales & Marketing which had 30% of the

tasks/month across all departments. Post-integration, AI-adopting employees in Operations showed a 15% improvement, those in Finance
showed 30% improvement, HR showed 15% improvement, and Sales & Marketing showed 30% improvement in their respective task
completion rates. Non-adopting employees saw no change in productivity.
